TalentPulse AI: D3 Exploratory Data Analysis¶

HireSense.ai candidate-profile extract (cleaned v1.1, 384,035 profiles) | XIME PGDM-BA05 | Capstone D3

Purpose. Before any model is built, find out what the data can and cannot support. Each analysis below answers a business question for the product (explainable candidate matching, market intelligence, offer risk) and tests a hypothesis that was written down before looking at the numbers.

How to run. Colab: Runtime > Run all. A file-upload box appears in the first code cell; choose candidate_profiles_clean_v1.1.csv.gz (output of the D2 cleaning). Outside Colab, set the environment variable DATA to the file path. Run time: about 2 minutes.

Privacy. The file is pseudonymised but still personal data. Do not share outputs outside the team, faculty and HireSense.ai.

1. Business questions and hypotheses (stated before the analysis)¶

Code Business question the product must answer
BQ1 Which profile signals are safe and useful to rank candidates on?
BQ2 Where is supply, and how scarce is a given skill profile? (market tab)
BQ3 What should a client budget, and where will an offer be competitive? (pay benchmark)
BQ4 Will semantic matching add value over keyword search? (core model)
BQ5 Where can bias or unrepresentative data mislead the ranker? (trust and compliance)
ID Hypothesis (written before analysis) Linked BQ Pass rule
H1 Experience is the dominant driver of pay: salary rises steadily with experience. BQ3 Spearman rho >= 0.6 and median salary rises in every band
H2 Automation and engineering skills (Selenium-stack, Python, Appium, CI/CD) carry a pay premium over manual-testing-only skills, after controlling for experience. BQ2, BQ3 Top skills at least +10% vs band median; manual skills below it
H3 Supply is concentrated in a few cities, and Bengaluru pays a premium at equal experience. BQ2, BQ3 Top 3 cities >= 50% of profiles; Bengaluru pay index >= 1.05
H4 The skill vocabulary is fragmented: exact keyword search hides a large share of relevant profiles. BQ4 > 100,000 distinct skill strings and synonym-aware search finds >= 25% more "Selenium" profiles
H5 Missing values are not random: blanks vary systematically with seniority. BQ1, BQ5 Chi-square p < 0.001 and spread >= 10 points for at least two fields
H6 Engagement (views) reflects profile completeness and recency, not merit, so it would bias a ranker. BQ1, BQ5 abs(rho) >= 0.3 with number of skills; fewer views for staler profiles
H7 The pool is dominated by QA/testing, so other role families are too thin for city-level analysis. BQ2, BQ5 QA >= 50% and some role-by-city cells below n = 30

2. Sanity checks on the cleaned data (re-check before trusting it)¶

D2 cleaning removed the large defects. Here we confirm the file is analysis-ready and look for residual problems.

In [2]:

3. Analysis dataset: derived fields used throughout¶

  • sal: salary in rupees, kept only when between Rs 1 lakh and Rs 1 crore (plausible range). Undisclosed and implausible values are excluded from pay analysis, never imputed.
  • rel: pay index = salary / median salary of the same experience band. 1.10 means 10% above peers of equal experience, which removes the experience effect.
  • act_days: days since last active, parsed from the relative label.
In [3]:
BANDS = ['0-2', '2-4', '4-6', '6-8', '8-10', '10-12', '12-15']
d['sal'] = d.salary_inr.where((d.salary_inr >= 1e5) & (d.salary_inr <= 1e7))
d['band'] = pd.Categorical(d.experience_band, BANDS, ordered=True)
band_med = d.groupby('band', observed=True).sal.median()
d['rel'] = d.sal / d.band.map(band_med).astype(float)
d['act_days'] = d.last_active_label.map(ACT)
d['city'] = d.current_city_std
TOP_CITIES = d.city.value_counts().head(8).index.tolist()
sk = d.key_skills.fillna('').str.lower().str.split('|').map(lambda l: [x for x in l if x])
N = len(d)
print(f'Analysis-ready: {N:,} profiles | pay analysis uses {d.sal.notna().sum():,} ({d.sal.notna().mean():.1%}) with a plausible disclosed salary')
display((band_med / 1e5).round(1).to_frame('median salary (Rs lakh)').T)

Analysis-ready: 384,035 profiles | pay analysis uses 362,266 (94.3%) with a plausible disclosed salary
band 0-2 2-4 4-6 6-8 8-10 10-12 12-15
median salary (Rs lakh) 3.50 5.00 7.50 11.30 15.00 19.40 21.90

4. Distributions: what does the pool look like?¶

Why it matters (BQ2, BQ5): a ranker can only be as good as the pool is broad. We check experience, geography, role mix, education, skills depth and pay.

In [4]:

5. H1: Is experience the dominant driver of pay? (BQ3)¶

A client setting a budget needs to know how much of pay is explained by experience alone.

In [7]:
m = d.dropna(subset=['sal', 'experience_years'])
rho, p = stats.spearmanr(m.experience_years, m.sal)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8.5, 3.8))
data = [m.loc[m.band == b, 'sal'] / 1e5 for b in BANDS]
bp = ax.boxplot(data, labels=BANDS, showfliers=False, patch_artist=True, medianprops=dict(color=RED, lw=2))
for b in bp['boxes']: b.set(facecolor='#DCE6F2', edgecolor=NAVY)
for i, b in enumerate(BANDS): ax.text(i + 1, ax.get_ylim()[1] * .95, f'n={len(data[i]):,}', ha='center', fontsize=7, color=GREY)
ax.set(title=f'Salary by experience band (Spearman rho = {rho:.2f})', xlabel='Experience band (years)', ylabel='Annual salary (Rs lakh)')
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
mono = all(np.diff(band_med.values) > 0)
H = {}
H['H1'] = ('Experience drives pay', f'rho = {rho:.2f}; medians rise in every band: {mono}', rho >= .6 and mono)
print(f'H1: rho = {rho:.2f} (p < 0.001), median salary rises in every band: {mono}  ->  {"SUPPORTED" if H["H1"][2] else "NOT SUPPORTED"}')
iqr = (m.groupby('band', observed=True).sal.quantile(.75) - m.groupby('band', observed=True).sal.quantile(.25)) / m.groupby('band', observed=True).sal.median()
print('Spread (IQR / median) by band:', iqr.round(2).to_dict())
print('INFERENCE: experience is a strong, usable criterion. But the spread inside each band is wide, so budget advice should be a range by band, not a single number.')

H1: rho = 0.73 (p < 0.001), median salary rises in every band: True  ->  SUPPORTED
Spread (IQR / median) by band: {'0-2': 0.49, '2-4': 0.54, '4-6': 0.6, '6-8': 0.66, '8-10': 0.69, '10-12': 0.6, '12-15': 0.56}
INFERENCE: experience is a strong, usable criterion. But the spread inside each band is wide, so budget advice should be a range by band, not a single number.

6. H2: Do skills carry a pay premium? (BQ2, BQ3)¶

We compare each skill's holders against peers of the same experience band using the pay index (1.00 = peers' median). Only skills with at least 3,000 holders are shown.

In [8]:
cnt = Counter(x for l in sk for x in l)
top_sk = [s for s, n in cnt.most_common(80) if n >= 3000][:60]
M = np.zeros((N, len(top_sk)), bool); ix = {s: i for i, s in enumerate(top_sk)}
for r, l in enumerate(sk):
    for x in l:
        j = ix.get(x)
        if j is not None: M[r, j] = True
prem = pd.DataFrame({'skill': top_sk, 'holders': M.sum(0), 'pay_index': [d.rel[M[:, i]].median() for i in range(len(top_sk))]}).sort_values('pay_index')
sel = pd.concat([prem.head(8), prem.tail(10)])
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8.5, 5))
ax.barh(sel.skill, sel.pay_index - 1, left=1, color=[RED if v < 1 else TEAL for v in sel.pay_index])
ax.axvline(1, color='k', lw=.8)
for i, (v, n) in enumerate(zip(sel.pay_index, sel.holders)): ax.text(v + (.004 if v >= 1 else -.004), i, f'{v:.2f}  (n={n:,})', va='center', ha='left' if v >= 1 else 'right', fontsize=7)
ax.set(title='Pay index by skill: lowest 8 and highest 10 (1.00 = same-experience peers)', xlabel='Pay index', xlim=(.8, 1.3))
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
hi, lo = prem.tail(10), prem.head(8)
H['H2'] = ('Skill pay premium', f'top skill {prem.iloc[-1].skill} {prem.iloc[-1].pay_index:.2f}; weakest {prem.iloc[0].skill} {prem.iloc[0].pay_index:.2f}', (hi.pay_index.median() >= 1.10) and (lo.pay_index.median() < 1.0))
print(f'Median pay index: top-10 skills {hi.pay_index.median():.2f}, bottom-8 skills {lo.pay_index.median():.2f}  ->  {"SUPPORTED" if H["H2"][2] else "NOT SUPPORTED"}')
print('INFERENCE: engineering-flavoured skills (SDET, Appium, Python, TypeScript, BDD, Jenkins) earn roughly 13-20% above peers; classic manual-testing skills sit about 10% below.')
print('           This is association, not causation (employer, city and seniority within a band also matter), so confidence is medium.')

Median pay index: top-10 skills 1.15, bottom-8 skills 0.90  ->  SUPPORTED
INFERENCE: engineering-flavoured skills (SDET, Appium, Python, TypeScript, BDD, Jenkins) earn roughly 13-20% above peers; classic manual-testing skills sit about 10% below.
           This is association, not causation (employer, city and seniority within a band also matter), so confidence is medium.

7. H3: Where is supply, and does location change pay? (BQ2, BQ3)¶

In [9]:

8. H4: Is the skill vocabulary fragmented? (BQ4)¶

If the same skill is written many ways, keyword search silently hides relevant people. This is the case for semantic matching.

In [10]:
tot = sum(cnt.values()); vc = np.array(sorted(cnt.values(), reverse=True))
cum = np.cumsum(vc) / tot
def has(pred): return sk.map(lambda l: any(pred(x) for x in l))
ex_sel = sk.map(lambda l: 'selenium' in l).sum(); any_sel = has(lambda x: 'selenium' in x).sum()
ex_api = sk.map(lambda l: 'api testing' in l).sum(); any_api = has(lambda x: ('api' in x and 'test' in x) or 'rest assured' in x or 'postman' in x or 'rest api' in x).sum()
ex_pw = sk.map(lambda l: 'playwright' in l).sum(); any_pw = has(lambda x: 'playwright' in x).sum()
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11.5, 3.8))
ax[0].plot(np.arange(1, len(cum) + 1), cum * 100, color=NAVY); ax[0].set_xscale('log')
for k in (50, 200, 1000): ax[0].scatter(k, cum[k - 1] * 100, color=RED, zorder=3); ax[0].text(k * 1.1, cum[k - 1] * 100 - 6, f'top {k}: {cum[k - 1]:.0%}', fontsize=8)
ax[0].set(title='Long tail: share of all skill mentions covered by the top-N skills', xlabel='Top N skills (log scale)', ylabel='Cumulative % of mentions')
lab = ['Selenium', 'API testing\n(incl. Postman, Rest Assured)', 'Playwright']
exact = [ex_sel, ex_api, ex_pw]; anyv = [any_sel, any_api, any_pw]
x = np.arange(3); ax[1].bar(x - .2, exact, .4, color=GREY, label='Exact keyword'); ax[1].bar(x + .2, anyv, .4, color=TEAL, label='Synonym / variant aware')
for i in range(3): ax[1].text(i + .2, anyv[i], f'+{anyv[i] / exact[i] - 1:.0%}', ha='center', va='bottom', fontsize=9, fontweight='bold')
ax[1].set_xticks(x); ax[1].set_xticklabels(lab); ax[1].legend(frameon=False); ax[1].set(title='Profiles found: exact keyword vs variant-aware', ylabel='Profiles')
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
gain = any_sel / ex_sel - 1
H['H4'] = ('Fragmented vocabulary', f'{len(cnt):,} distinct skill strings; Selenium +{gain:.0%} with variants', len(cnt) > 100000 and gain >= .25)
print(f'H4: {len(cnt):,} distinct skill strings; the top 200 cover {cum[199]:.0%} of mentions; variant-aware Selenium search finds {gain:.0%} more profiles  ->  {"SUPPORTED" if H["H4"][2] else "NOT SUPPORTED"}')
print('INFERENCE: a keyword portal misses about four in ten relevant Selenium profiles. A skill taxonomy plus embedding-based matching is the single strongest product differentiator, and the data proves the gap.')

H4: 108,043 distinct skill strings; the top 200 cover 71% of mentions; variant-aware Selenium search finds 71% more profiles  ->  SUPPORTED
INFERENCE: a keyword portal misses about four in ten relevant Selenium profiles. A skill taxonomy plus embedding-based matching is the single strongest product differentiator, and the data proves the gap.

el = d.groupby('education_level').agg(n=('sal', 'size'), med=('sal', 'median')); el = el[el.n > 5000].sort_values('med')
ax[2].barh(el.index, el.med / 1e5, color=TEAL); ax[2].set(title='Median salary by education level', xlabel='Rs lakh'); ax[2].tick_params(axis='y', labelsize=7)

10. Representativeness and bias checks (repeated on the cleaned data)¶

D2 flagged the risks on the raw schema. Here they are re-measured on the cleaned 384,035 profiles, with statistical tests and effect sizes.

10a. H5: Are missing values random? (BQ1, BQ5)¶

A blank field cannot be read as "does not qualify". We test whether blanks track seniority or city.

In [14]:
d['blank_current_role'] = d.current_role.isna(); d['blank_previous_role'] = d.previous_role.isna()
d['blank_pref_loc'] = d.preferred_locations.isna(); d['salary_undisclosed'] = d.salary_zero_flag.astype(bool)
FIELDS = {'blank_current_role': 'Current role', 'blank_previous_role': 'Previous role', 'blank_pref_loc': 'Preferred locations', 'salary_undisclosed': 'Salary undisclosed'}
def cramers_v(ct):
    chi2 = stats.chi2_contingency(ct)[0]; n = ct.values.sum(); return np.sqrt(chi2 / (n * (min(ct.shape) - 1)))
rows = []
for c, lab in FIELDS.items():
    ct = pd.crosstab(d.band, d[c]); rate = ct[True] / ct.sum(1) * 100
    rows.append((lab, stats.chi2_contingency(ct)[1], cramers_v(ct), rate.max() - rate.min(), rate.idxmin(), rate.idxmax()))
miss = pd.DataFrame(rows, columns=['field', 'chi2 p-value', "Cramer's V", 'spread (pts)', 'lowest band', 'highest band']); display(miss)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 3.8))
for c, lab in FIELDS.items(): ax[0].plot(BANDS, d.groupby('band', observed=True)[c].mean().reindex(BANDS) * 100, marker='o', label=lab)
ax[0].set(title='Share of blank values by experience band', xlabel='Experience band (years)', ylabel='% blank'); ax[0].legend(frameon=False, fontsize=8)
cm_ = d[d.city.isin(TOP_CITIES[:6])].groupby('city')[list(FIELDS)].mean().reindex(TOP_CITIES[:6]) * 100; cm_.columns = list(FIELDS.values())
sns.heatmap(cm_, annot=True, fmt='.0f', cmap='Oranges', ax=ax[1], cbar_kws={'label': '% blank'}); ax[1].set(title='Share of blank values by city', ylabel='')
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
n_ok = int(((miss['chi2 p-value'] < .001) & (miss['spread (pts)'] >= 10)).sum())
H['H5'] = ('Non-random missingness', f'{n_ok} of 4 fields differ by >=10 pts across bands (p<0.001)', n_ok >= 2)
print(f'H5: {n_ok} of 4 fields show a >=10-point spread across experience bands  ->  {"SUPPORTED" if H["H5"][2] else "NOT SUPPORTED"}')
print('INFERENCE: juniors leave current role and previous role blank far more often, and seniors leave preferred locations blank. Scoring on these fields would systematically penalise one group. Treat "not stated" as unknown, re-weight, and never reward or punish it.')

10b. H6: Does engagement reflect merit or exposure? (BQ1, BQ5)¶

If views track completeness and recency, ranking on them would reward visibility, not fit.

In [15]:

# Concrete exposure check: who would a popularity ranker surface? (top 1% by views vs the whole pool)
top1 = d[d.total_views >= d.total_views.quantile(.99)]
def comp(col, order=None):
    a = top1[col].value_counts(normalize=True) * 100; b = d[col].value_counts(normalize=True) * 100
    t = pd.DataFrame({'top 1% by views': a, 'whole pool': b}).fillna(0)
    return t.reindex(order) if order is not None else t
cb = comp('band', BANDS); cci = comp('city').loc[TOP_CITIES[:6]]
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 3.4))
cb.plot(kind='bar', ax=ax[0], color=[RED, GREY], width=.75); ax[0].set(title='Experience mix: top 1% by views vs pool', xlabel='Experience band (years)', ylabel='% of profiles'); ax[0].tick_params(axis='x', rotation=0); ax[0].legend(frameon=False, fontsize=8)
cci.plot(kind='bar', ax=ax[1], color=[RED, GREY], width=.75); ax[1].set(title='City mix: top 1% by views vs pool', xlabel='', ylabel='% of profiles'); ax[1].tick_params(axis='x', rotation=25); ax[1].legend(frameon=False, fontsize=8)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
ratio_b = (cb['top 1% by views'] / cb['whole pool'])
print(f'Selection-rate ratio (top-1% share / pool share) by band: {ratio_b.round(2).to_dict()}')
print('INFERENCE: a popularity-driven shortlist over-selects mid-to-senior profiles and under-selects juniors; fairness monitoring must track selection-rate ratios like these on every shortlist.')

10c. H7: Is the pool dominated by QA, leaving other segments too thin? (BQ2, BQ5)¶

We apply the project rule that a subgroup needs at least n = 30 to be reported.

In [17]:
cells = pd.crosstab(d.role_family, d.city.where(d.city.isin(TOP_CITIES[:6]))).drop(index='Unclassified (no role text)', errors='ignore')
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 3.8))
sns.heatmap(np.log10(cells + 1), annot=cells.values, fmt=',', cmap='Blues', ax=ax, cbar_kws={'label': 'log10(profiles + 1)'}, annot_kws={'size': 7})
for (i, j) in zip(*np.where(cells.values < 30)): ax.add_patch(plt.Rectangle((j, i), 1, 1, fill=False, edgecolor=RED, lw=2))

qa = (d.role_family == 'QA / Testing').mean(); thin = int((cells.values < 30).sum())
fine = pd.crosstab([d.role_family, d.band], d.city.where(d.city.isin(TOP_CITIES[:6]))).drop(index='Unclassified (no role text)', level=0, errors='ignore')
fine_thin, fine_n = int((fine.values < 30).sum()), fine.size
partA, partB = qa >= .5, thin > 0
H['H7'] = ('QA-dominated pool', f'QA {qa:.1%}; role x city cells < 30: {thin} of {cells.size}; role x band x city: {fine_thin} of {fine_n}', False, 'PARTLY SUPPORTED')
print(f'H7 part A (QA >= 50%): {qa:.1%} -> {partA}. Part B (some role x city cells < 30): {thin} of {cells.size} -> {partB}  =>  PARTLY SUPPORTED')
print(f'Finer cut (role x experience band x city): {fine_thin} of {fine_n} cells have fewer than 30 profiles.')
print('INFERENCE: dominance is confirmed, but every role-by-city cell is large enough to report. Thin cells appear only at finer cuts, so non-QA families can be reported by city, not by city and band together. Evaluate first on QA/testing, where data is densest.')

Each row: what we found, the number behind it, what it means for the decision, and how sure we are. Confidence = High when the effect is large, tested and consistent; Medium when it is observational or rests on a proxy; Low when data is thin.

13. What matters most, and how it shapes modelling¶

  1. Fragmented skills are the opening for semantic matching (H4). Keyword search misses roughly four in ten relevant profiles. The model must work on a skill taxonomy plus embeddings, evaluated against exact-match and weights-only baselines.
  2. Rank on role, skills and experience; keep engagement and disclosure out (H5, H6). Views, downloads, recency, salary disclosure and location preference are biased by profile length and seniority. They stay descriptive, and "not stated" is re-weighted, never penalised.
  3. Experience and skills set price; city sets supply (H1-H3). The market tab and offer advice should be built on experience band, skill premium and city, shown as ranges with sample sizes.
  4. Scope the first release to QA/testing talent in metros (H7). QA is 62% of the pool. Role-by-city views are reliable, but finer slices (role x band x city) are not, so evaluation and fairness checks follow the n >= 30 rule.
  5. Close the data gaps before the offer-risk model. Expected CTC, notice period, gender (with consent) and hiring-demand data are absent from our extract; request them from HireSense.ai.
